title: Early Lý Dynasty
capsule: The Early Lý dynasty ruled the independent Vietnamese state of Vạn Xuân from 544 to 602 CE, representing the first successful Vietnamese bid for self-rule after six centuries of Chinese Han domination. Its founder Lý Bí (Lý Nam Đế) rebelled against Liang Chinese rule in 542, declared the kingdom of Vạn Xuân in 544, and assumed imperial title at Long Biên (near modern Hanoi). Internal succession conflict between Triệu Quang Phục and Lý Phật Tử fractured the state from 548 onward, though Lý Phật Tử reunified it by 571 and reigned until 602, when a Sui dynasty army of approximately 100,000 troops overran the kingdom and reimposed Chinese rule for another three and a half centuries.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Political narrative is reasonably well attested through later Vietnamese annals (Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư) and Chinese dynastic histories, but territorial mapping of Vạn Xuân's control beyond the Red River delta is speculative.
